questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman presented with fevers and a swollen right eyelid with a red eye, purulent drainage, tearing, and some blurriness. She was normally well and did not take any regular medications. She had no known drug allergies. She reported contact with a person that had recent smallpox vaccination as he had just joined the military. On exam, she had periorbital edema and redness on the right eyelid with a cutaneous vesicle present. She had visual acuity of 20/40 on the right. There was no inflammation of the cornea. Right submandibular and preauricular lymphadenopathy were also present. Conjunctival scrapings were sent for microbiology.
questions.lead_in: What is the best treatment option?
questions.explanation: Vaccinia immunoglobulin and topical trifluridine The patient has vaccine-associated preseptal cellulitis and conjunctivitis from contact with the military recruit who had recent smallpox immunization. It is important to remember that patients who receive smallpox vaccination may shed live virus while the vaccination site is healing. This typically lasts until separation of the scab which is usually 2–3 weeks after the vaccination. Vaccinia immunoglobulin and topical trifluridine are the treatment of choice. More severe cases warrant immunoglobulin, and it does help decrease shedding of virus. While vancomycin and a cephalosporin would be reasonable for the preseptal cellulitis, it would not address the conjunctivitis in this case. The vesicle points toward a viral etiology. Azithromycin would be for suspected Chlamydia; however, the clinical scenario is not consistent with such given the vesicle and recent contact with a contact of a recently vaccinated person.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q10

questions.question: Orbital cellulitis with potential thrombosis of the cavernous sinus

parts.text: Indicate 3 signs or symptoms that point to orbital cellulitis rather than pre-septal
Name the 4 potentially affected nerves in thrombosis of the cavernous sinus and name a clinical sign for each

cohort_answer.text:
Three signs/symptoms: Ophthalmoplegia; Pain with eye movements; Proptosis; Diplopia. Orbital cellulitis: infection of contents of the orbit (fat and ocular muscles), distinguished from Preseptal cellulitis (sometimes called periorbital cellulitis): infection of the anterior portion of the eyelid. Neither infection involves the globe itself. Micro: Staph aureus, Strep pyogenes, H.flu, Fungi (mucorales, aspergillus), Mycobacteria (TB). Complications: Subperiosteal abscess; Orbital abscess; Epidural or subdural empyema; Brain abscess; Meningitis; Cavernous sinus thrombosis
Four nerves and clinical signs: CN III – Eye turned downward and outward. Ptosis. CN IV – Eye turned upwards and inwards. Limited adduction and intorsion (Superior oblique weakness). CN V – Loss of facial sensation. CN VI – Right eye turned medially. Inability to abduct eye (Lateral rectus weakness)

questions.question: Preseptal vs orbital cellulitis. (adult version)

parts.text: 4 symptoms that point towards it being orbital cellulitis vs. preseptal cellulitis

questions.model_answer: Four features favoring orbital (vs. preseptal) cellulitis: (1) proptosis (2) ophthalmoplegia and/or pain with eye movement (3) decreased visual acuity (4) chemosis and/or an afferent pupillary defect - in preseptal disease the eye movements are full and painless and vision is normal.

questions.question: PM Q23. Name 3 signs/symptoms of orbital cellulitis that differentiate it from preseptal cellulitis.

parts.text: Name 3 signs/symptoms of orbital cellulitis that differentiate it from preseptal cellulitis
b) In the setting of cavernous sinus thrombosis as a complication, name 4 cranial nerves that are affected and list a sign or symptom in the context of orbital cellulitis for each.

cohort_answer.text:
Proptosis; Pain with movement of the eye; Impairment of ocular eye movement (upward gaze); Loss of visual acuity, double vision. Orbital cellulitis commonly caused by sinusitis; pre-septal most commonly secondary to skin infections around eye/eyelid
Cranial nerve III (oculomotor): ophthalmoplegia, paresis out/down, ptosis, dilated pupil; CN IV (trochlear): downward gaze impairment especially adducted eye; CN VI (abducens): lateral gaze impairment; CN V (trigeminal V1/V2): sensory loss of forehead/mid cheeks. Vision loss caused by venous congestion and ischemia. Contralateral inflammation: lid swelling, proptosis, ophthalmoplegia

questions.question: Guy has orbital cellulitis.

parts.text: 3 symptoms to distinguish from presentation.
What 4 nerves are involved if cavernous thrombosis and what manifestation of each?

questions.model_answer:
a) Three distinguishing symptoms of orbital cellulitis: proptosis, ophthalmoplegia with pain on eye movement, and decreased visual acuity (chemosis and afferent pupillary defect also qualify).
b) Four cranial nerves involved in cavernous sinus thrombosis and their manifestations: CN III (oculomotor) - ptosis, mydriasis, eye deviated 'down and out', ophthalmoplegia; CN IV (trochlear) - vertical/torsional diplopia from superior oblique weakness; CN VI (abducens) - lateral gaze palsy/failure of abduction (often the earliest sign, as CN VI runs freely through the sinus); CN V1 (ophthalmic division of trigeminal) - forehead and periorbital sensory loss.

questions.question: Orbital cellulitis

parts.text: List 3 clinical findings that increase the likelihood of orbital cellulitis.
Which 4 cranial nerves could be involved if there was a cavernous sinus thrombus, and what sign or symptom would each have?

questions.model_answer:
a) Three clinical findings increasing likelihood of orbital cellulitis: proptosis, ophthalmoplegia/pain with eye movement, and decreased visual acuity (or afferent pupillary defect/chemosis).
b) Four cranial nerves with cavernous sinus thrombus and their signs: CN III - ptosis, mydriasis, 'down and out' eye position; CN IV - vertical diplopia (superior oblique palsy); CN VI - lateral gaze palsy/abduction failure; CN V1 - forehead/periorbital sensory loss.

questions.question: Orbital cellulitis

parts.text: What anatomical structure separates preseptal and orbital cellulitis
What are 5 clinical differences between orbital and pre-septal cellulitis
In sinusitis, which sinus is most likely to have extension to the eye
If the patient develops ipsilateral lateral gaze palsy, what complication do you worry about?

questions.model_answer:
a) Anatomical structure separating preseptal from orbital cellulitis: the orbital septum.
b) Five clinical differences: (1) proptosis - present in orbital, absent in preseptal (2) ophthalmoplegia/pain with eye movement - present in orbital, absent in preseptal (3) decreased visual acuity - can occur in orbital, normal in preseptal (4) chemosis - more prominent in orbital (5) afferent pupillary defect - can occur in orbital (optic nerve compromise), absent in preseptal; preseptal disease is limited to eyelid/periorbital swelling and erythema with full, painless extraocular movements.
c) Sinus most likely to extend to the eye: the ethmoid sinus (thin lamina papyracea medially, with dehiscences allowing direct spread).
d) Ipsilateral lateral gaze palsy (CN VI palsy): raises concern for cavernous sinus thrombosis (CN VI runs freely within the sinus and is often the first affected).

parts.text: Anatomic landmark separating orbital and pre-septal
5 symptoms
Highest risk sinus and why
Ipsilateral eye palsy, what is the diagnosis

cohort_answer.text:
Anatomic landmark: The orbital septum - a thin, fibrous membrane arising from orbital periosteum, a barrier between the lids and the orbit. Infections anterior to the septum are preseptal (lid only), posterior to the septum are orbital (fat, muscles of orbit).
5 symptoms: Ophthalmoplegia (paralysis, absent in pre-septal); proptosis (absent in pre-septal); fever (more common in children); pain with eye movement; vision can be decreased (absent in pre-septal); afferent pupillary defect; leukocytosis (more common in children).
Highest risk sinus and why: Ethmoid. The orbit is surrounded by sinuses (frontal superiorly, maxillary inferiorly, ethmoid medially). The medial orbital wall is made from the lateral ethmoid sinus wall formed by a paper-thin lamina papyracea, contains multiple foramina for nerves/blood vessels, and some people have natural defects called Zuckerkandl dehiscences. For these anatomic reasons, ethmoid sinusitis is the most common cause of sinus-related orbital infection.
Ipsilateral eye palsy diagnosis: Septic cavernous sinus thrombophlebitis. The venous drainage of the eye and face is through the cavernous sinus, risk for cavernous venous sinus syndrome; the cavernous sinus is a venous plexus extending to the opposite side, allowing spread of infection with bilateral cranial neuropathies typical. Suspect this diagnosis with involvement of CN III, IV, VI, V2 (maxillary) branch, or bilateral involvement of cranial neuropathies.

questions.question:
Q32 (2017)
5 year old child has orbital cellulitis complicated by cavernous sinus thrombosis.

parts.text: A) List 3 findings that suggest orbital vs pre-orbital cellulitis?
B) Fill this table regarding which cranial nerves are affected by cavernous sinus thrombosis and 4 common symptoms and signs: CN III (oculomotor), IV (trochlear), V (trigeminal), VI (abducens)

cohort_answer.text:
A) Proptosis, Pain on extraocular movements, Ophthalmoplegia, Diplopia, Chemosis.

B) III (oculomotor): Downward (SO4), outward gaze (LR6), dilated pupil. IV (trochlear): Hypertropia, head tilt. V (trigeminal): Deviation of the jaw, paresthesias, pain, inability to chew or bite down. VI (abducens): esotropia.

parts.text: A) List the organisms likely involved
B) Treatment
C) Further investigations

cohort_answer.text:
Group A Streptococcus; S. aureus (including MRSA); S. pneumoniae; H. influenzae; Moraxella; S. anginosus; Oral anaerobes
CTX + Flagyl +/- Clox or Vanco. (UTD: Vanco + CTX/Cefotaxime + metronidazole for anaerobic coverage until intracranial involvement excluded; fluoroquinolone + vanco if penicillin/cephalosporin allergic)
BCx; CT Head+Orbits (consider MRI in kids due to radiation); consider LP if suspecting meningitis; ENT/Ophtho consult +/- neurosurgery and plastics

questions.question: A patient presents with a CN palsy and cavernous sinus thrombosis.

parts.text: What clinical features differentiate orbital from preorbital cellulitis (I think they asked for 4)

cohort_answer.text: Proptosis, diplopia, pain with extraocular movement, chemosis, ophthalmoplegia.

parts.text: What is the anatomic structure that differentiates between preseptal and orbital cellulitis (0.5)
Name 5 clinical signs/symptoms that would suggest orbital cellulitis over preseptal (2.5)
Sinusitis of which sinus leads to highest risk for orbital cellulitis and why (1)
Patient now has ipsilateral lateral nerve palsy. What complication are you worried about (0.5)

cohort_answer.text: Anatomic structure: Orbital septum - thin fibrous membrane serving as barrier between superficial lids and orbit; infections anterior to septum are preseptal, posterior are orbital (Mandell's); preseptal involves only lids not the orbit, orbital cellulitis involves soft tissues (fat, muscle) within bony orbit. Signs of orbital cellulitis: Proptosis; Painful extraocular eye movement; Ophthalmoplegia; Diplopia; Chemosis. Highest risk sinus: Ethmoid - separated from orbit by thin lamina papyracea (medial wall of orbit), contains multiple foramina for nerves/vessels, some people have natural defects; nearly all periosteal abscesses secondary to ethmoid sinusitis. Complication to rule out with cranial nerve palsy: Cavernous sinus thrombosis - spread to opposite eye through cavernous sinus usually within 24-48 hours of initial unilateral orbital findings; may present with bilateral findings or signs of bilateral neuropathies of CN III, IV, VI without lid edema/erythema typical of orbital cellulitis, especially from skin infections of middle third of face or dental infections
